data.content_ref: inline:The target's mechanism claims the preference for better-corroborated theories is 'rational because it maximizes the opportunity for future falsification (severe testing), thereby accelerating error elimination.' This justification invokes error elimination as a normatively valuable goal, but the target simultaneously concedes that the procedure 'cannot guarantee progress toward truth, only the avoidance of known falsities.' This creates an internal tension: error elimination is only epistemically significant if eliminating errors brings one closer to truth (i.e., it has a truth-approximation function). The target explicitly severs that connection, reducing 'error elimination' to the trivial act of discarding already-falsified theories—a description that provides no normative reason to prefer among surviving (unfalsified) theories. A preference that serves a goal emptied of its only natural normative grounding is not 'defensible' or 'rational' in any substantive sense; it is merely a convention the target itself labels 'purely procedural conventionalism.' The claim thus smuggles in the normative force of 'error elimination' while denying the truth-connection that alone makes error elimination normatively significant rather than merely descriptive. This is not addressed by any of the three listed counterconditions, which concern verisimilitude, induction, and psychological necessity respectively—not the normative vacuity of an error-elimination goal divorced from truth-approximation.
